narrative.text:
# payment — Solution Architecture Document

## Executive summary

**What this is.** This design describes how an accredited outside company, such as a merchant's payment provider, can start a one-off domestic payment from a retail customer's bank account, with the customer's own approval. The provider creates the payment request, the customer approves it on the bank's redirected web pages, and the bank checks the payment, takes the money once and hands the payment on for execution [VS-MERCHANT] [SVC-INIT] [SVC-AUTH].

**Why it matters.** Providers need a standard, dependable way to start payments, and customers need to stay in control of their money. The requirements ask for a consistent API version, for consent that expires, and for personal and account information to be protected [R-18] [R-03] [R-16].

```desnre ax-glance
```

**What it sets out to achieve.**

- **The customer stays in control.** Only an authorised consent can be used to submit one payment, unauthorised consent lapses after 24 hours, and a decline or failed authentication never debits an account [R-04] [R-23] [R-12].
- **Each payment is taken once.** A repeated request does not create a second debit, and exactly one ledger debit is made per accepted payment [R-05] [R-09].
- **Bad payments are stopped first.** Data and account are validated, and a risk screening decision is applied before debit and hand-off [R-06] [R-07] [R-08].
- **Status can be seen.** The provider can retrieve the payment and its status, and a payment accepted for execution is not shown as completed at another bank [R-11] [R-19].
- **The service is dependable.** The targets are availability of at least 99.95% monthly, read p95 latency of at most 500 ms at 200 requests per second, and recovery within 30 minutes (all marked fictional targets) [R-13] [R-14] [R-15].

**The outcome.** A payment initiation service built on three banking building blocks (payment order initiation, party authentication and fraud evaluation), running on the bank's deployments with explicit segment boundaries and managed secrets [R-20].

**Benefits.** For customers: clear consent and protection before any debit. For providers and merchants: one standard connection. For the bank: checked payments and auditable decisions [R-17]. The design records no business-case figures (volumes, revenue or cost), so benefits are stated from what the requirements ask, not measured.

**What is still open.** Six security details are unknown, fifteen warnings are recorded, and the reasons behind decisions and failure handling are not in the design (sections 5 and 10).

## 1. Purpose of this document

This document describes the payment design as a solution architecture for a solution architect. It sets out what the design covers, the requirements it rests on, the target architecture across business, service-domain, application, technology and security views, and what the design does not yet say. It is written from the design's records only; where a record is silent, the text says so. Its subject is the Merchant payment value stream [VS-MERCHANT].

The figures below count the design's records and connections.

```desnre figures
```

## 2. Scope

**In scope.** The value stream Merchant payment [VS-MERCHANT], with its three stages Consent [ST-CONSENT], Payment submission [ST-SUBMIT] and Status enquiry [ST-STATUS]. The capability Domestic payment initiation [CAP-PAY] groups Customer payment consent [CAP-CONSENT] and Payment risk control [CAP-RISK]. Eight business processes, all assigned to the Bank — account servicing role [ROLE-BANK], carry the work: Capture consent [PROC-CONSENT], Authenticate and authorise [PROC-AUTH], Receive the payment [PROC-SUBMIT], Validate data and account [PROC-VALIDATE], Screen fraud [PROC-RISK], Post one debit [PROC-DEBIT], Hand off for execution [PROC-HANDOFF] and Respond to status enquiries [PROC-STATUS]. The design serves the Accredited third-party provider [ACTOR-TPP], the Merchant [ACTOR-MERCHANT] and the Retail customer [ACTOR-CUSTOMER] through the Business initiation service [SVC-INIT] and the Consent authorisation service [SVC-AUTH], over the Provider API channel [IF-TPP] and the Redirected authorisation web channel [IF-WEB]. The offering is the Retail account [PROD-ACCOUNT].

**Out of scope.** Only redirect authorisation is designed; the requirement for hybrid redirect and decoupled (CIBA) authorisation says the full regulated implementation remains outside the first stage [R-21]. The design records no other explicit out-of-scope list.

## 3. Goals, objectives and constraints

All 24 requirements are priority "must". They are grouped here by what they constrain.

**Consent and authorisation.** The third party creates a one-off domestic payment consent and receives a bank-generated identifier [R-01]. The bank authenticates the customer through the redirect flow and accepts or rejects the complete consent [R-02]. Unauthorised consent lasts 24 hours and expired consent cannot be used [R-03] [R-23]. Only an authorised consent may be used to submit one payment [R-04]. A decline, failed authentication or expired consent does not debit an account [R-12]. Hybrid redirect and decoupled (CIBA) authorisation is required but only redirect is designed [R-21].

**Payment correctness.** The same request does not create a second debit under supported idempotent replay [R-05]. Data use NZD and valid domestic account identification [R-06]. Account eligibility and funds are checked before posting [R-07]. A risk screening decision is applied before debit and hand-off [R-08]. Exactly one ledger debit is committed per accepted payment [R-09]. The accepted instruction is handed to the execution boundary [R-10].

**Status and information release.** The third party can retrieve the payment and its status [R-11]. A payment accepted for execution is not represented as completed at another bank [R-19]. A debtor-account read is only returned where DebtorAccountRelease is true [R-24].

**Service levels.** Availability of at least 99.95% monthly [R-13]; read p95 latency at most 500 ms at 200 requests per second [R-14]; recovery time at most 30 minutes and recovery point at most 5 minutes [R-15]. Each is described in the records as a fictional target.

**Security, audit and standards.** Personal and account information is protected and access is scoped [R-16]. Decisions are correlated and auditable [R-17]. Deployments have explicit segment boundaries, private persistence routes and managed secrets [R-20]. The bank uses version 2.3.3 consistently for consent and payment API resources [R-18], and throttling (429) and participant identification follow the MBIE-modified v2.3.3 requirements [R-22].

## 4. Compliance

**Standards named by the records.** The API follows the NZ Banking Data standard v2.3.3 [IFC-PAYMENT-INITIATION], and requirements refer to version 2.3.3 and the MBIE-modified v2.3.3 requirements [R-18] [R-22]. The three service domains are BIAN 14.0.0 [SD-PAYMENT-ORDER-INITIATION] [SD-PARTY-AUTHENTICATION] [SD-FRAUD-EVALUATION]. The key custody software conforms to the key-store part of the Payment initiation pattern [SYS-KMS].

**Security frameworks.** The design's security controls are each a NIST SP 800-53 control with a CSF 2.0 function and category, for example Customer authentication as IA-2 with function PR and category PR.AA [SEC-IA2] and Audit events as AU-12 with function DE and category DE.CM [SEC-AU12]. Its threats are classified by STRIDE, for example a third party impersonated at the API as category S [THR-SPOOF-TPP]. All 15 controls have implementation status "planned" (section 9.7).

## 5. Risks and issues

The design records nine threats, each with a STRIDE category, likelihood, impact and a treatment of "mitigate". Each is mitigated by at least one control. They are listed in the table below and described in section 9.7.

```desnre table threats
```

The highest-rated are those with high impact and medium likelihood: impersonation of a third party at the API [THR-SPOOF-TPP], disclosure of consent and account data [THR-DISCLOSE-CONSENT], a payment order initiated without authority (S and E) [THR-POI-UNAUTH], and compromise of customer credentials (S and I) [THR-PA-CREDS]. Other threats carry low likelihood and high impact: tampering with a payment on its way to execution [THR-TAMPER-HANDOFF], alteration of an accepted order [THR-POI-TAMPER] and bypass of fraud screening (T and E) [THR-FE-BYPASS]. Two are medium on both: a customer denying consent [THR-REPUDIATE-CONSENT] and a flood at the internet edge [THR-FLOOD-EDGE].

Open issues the data shows: a debtor-account read operation has no path or payload fields yet [API-DEBTOR-READ]; four deployments have no platform recorded [DEP-CONSENT] [DEP-PAYHUB] [DEP-RISK] [DEP-NOTIFY]; and two links proposed by the design engine were rejected [MAP-033] [MAP-034]. The design does not record failure handling, such as what happens on a fraud rejection or a failed posting.

## 6. Baseline architecture

The design holds no baseline architecture. The records, such as the Merchant payment value stream [VS-MERCHANT] and the Payments hub [APP-PAYHUB], have lifecycle status "planned", and no existing system is recorded as being replaced.

## 7. Rationale and justification

The design records no decisions with reasons: records carry no rationale text. The only reasoning visible is the evidence on connections, which cites design-document sections and an engine rationale. Choices a reviewer would expect to see justified are: one application component per service domain, with Payments hub realising Payment Order Initiation [SD-PAYMENT-ORDER-INITIATION REALIZED_BY APP-PAYHUB]; the shared three-node compute for four applications [NODE-APP]; the event-based hand-off [APP-PAYHUB triggering EVT-HANDOFF]; and the single production location [LOC-NZ]. The design does not say why these were chosen.

The engine rejected two proposed connections: API ingress realising Payment Order Initiation [MAP-033] and Fraud Evaluation supporting Payment risk control [MAP-034]. The records give the engine's rationale for proposing them but not the reason for rejecting them.

## 8. Mapping to the architecture repository

The repository table lists the design's records by layer, and the layered view shows how they connect across the four layers, for example Receive the payment using Payment Order Initiation [MAP-001], which is realised by the Payments hub [MAP-005] and deployed as [MAP-014]. The design holds 87 connections between layers: 85 approved and 2 rejected. The rejected ones are left out of the views.

```desnre table repository
```

```desnre ax-layered
```

## 9. Target architecture

The target architecture, layer by layer.

### 9.1 Conceptual view

In concept, an accredited provider [ACTOR-TPP] asks the bank, through the Provider API channel [IF-TPP], to create a payment consent. The retail customer [ACTOR-CUSTOMER] approves it on a redirected web channel [IF-WEB]. The bank, acting in its account servicing role [ROLE-BANK], then submits, validates, screens, debits and hands off the payment, and answers status enquiries. The diagram shows the actors, roles, channels and services and how they relate.

```desnre ax-business
```

### 9.2 Business architecture

**Value stream.** Merchant payment [VS-MERCHANT] flows from Consent [ST-CONSENT] to Payment submission [ST-SUBMIT] [ST-CONSENT flow ST-SUBMIT], then to Status enquiry [ST-STATUS] [ST-SUBMIT flow ST-STATUS]. Consent is realised by Capture consent [PROC-CONSENT] and Authenticate and authorise [PROC-AUTH]. Submission is realised by five processes: Receive the payment [PROC-SUBMIT], Validate data and account [PROC-VALIDATE], Screen fraud [PROC-RISK], Post one debit [PROC-DEBIT] and Hand off for execution [PROC-HANDOFF]. Status enquiry is realised by Respond to status enquiries [PROC-STATUS].

**Process chain.** The processes flow in sequence from consent capture to status [PROC-CONSENT flow PROC-AUTH] [PROC-AUTH flow PROC-SUBMIT] [PROC-SUBMIT flow PROC-VALIDATE] [PROC-VALIDATE flow PROC-RISK] [PROC-RISK flow PROC-DEBIT] [PROC-DEBIT flow PROC-HANDOFF] [PROC-HANDOFF flow PROC-STATUS]. All are automated and all are assigned to the Bank — account servicing role [ROLE-BANK].

**Capabilities.** Domestic payment initiation [CAP-PAY] aggregates Customer payment consent [CAP-CONSENT] and Payment risk control [CAP-RISK]. Only the top capability has an approved connection to a service domain: it is supported by Payment Order Initiation [MAP-004]. A proposed link from Payment risk control to Fraud Evaluation was rejected.

**Services and channels.** The Business initiation service [SVC-INIT] serves the provider [ACTOR-TPP] and the Merchant [ACTOR-MERCHANT]; the Consent authorisation service [SVC-AUTH] serves the Retail customer [ACTOR-CUSTOMER]. The Retail account [PROD-ACCOUNT] aggregates the initiation service [PROD-ACCOUNT aggregation SVC-INIT].

```desnre ax-capabilities
```

Four processes have no connection to a service domain: Capture consent [PROC-CONSENT], Validate data and account [PROC-VALIDATE], Post one debit [PROC-DEBIT] and Hand off for execution [PROC-HANDOFF]. Of these, Post one debit has a security control [SEC-AC5].

### 9.3 Service architecture (BIAN)

The design uses three BIAN 14.0.0 service domains. **Payment Order Initiation** [SD-PAYMENT-ORDER-INITIATION] uses the Transact functional pattern, and is used by Receive the payment [MAP-001] and Respond to status enquiries [MAP-002]. It is realised by the Payments hub [MAP-005]. Its service groups are Payment Order Initiation Transaction, Compliance, Confirmation and Order Initiation, and its control record is Payment Order Initiation Transaction [CR-PAYMENT-ORDER-INITIATION]. **Party Authentication** [SD-PARTY-AUTHENTICATION] uses the Assess pattern, is used by Authenticate and authorise [MAP-003] and is realised by Identity [MAP-006]. Its seven service groups are Party Authentication Assessment, Password, Question, Document, Device, Biometric and Behavior. **Fraud Evaluation** [SD-FRAUD-EVALUATION] uses the Assess pattern, is used by Screen fraud [MAP-031] and is realised by the Fraud service [MAP-032]. It has three service groups: Fraud Evaluation Assessment, Rule Setsand Decision Trees and Models.

At operation level, Create domestic payment implements the Initiate operation [MAP-007] and Read domestic payment implements the Retrieve operation [MAP-008]. The design proposed API ingress realising Payment Order Initiation but that connection was rejected [MAP-033].

```desnre ax-bian
```

```desnre table bian
```

The completeness checks advise that none of the three domains is composed into a BIAN business domain; this is advice, not a recorded defect.

### 9.4 Data architecture

The design holds four data entities, all stored in the Managed database [SYS-DB] except the security event log, which is stored in Audit and metrics [SYS-OBS].

**ConsentLedger** [DATA-CONSENT] holds each consent: identifier, third party, customer, status, instruction and end-to-end identifiers, amount, currency, creditor and debtor accounts and expiry. It is flagged as holding personal information, and customer_id, creditor_account and debtor_account are marked personal and confidential [F-CONSENT-CUSTOMER-ID] [F-CONSENT-CREDITOR-ACCOUNT] [F-CONSENT-DEBTOR-ACCOUNT]. Its status takes the values AwaitingAuthorisation, Authorised, Rejected and Consumed [F-CONSENT-STATUS]. It is stored in the database [DATA-CONSENT STORED_IN SYS-DB].

**PaymentLedger** [DATA-PAYMENT] holds each payment with its consent_id, amount, currency, ledger posting id, hand-off id and creation time. Its consent_id refers to ConsentLedger [F-PAYMENT-CONSENT-ID]. Payment status takes the values Pending, Rejected, AcceptedSettlementInProcess and AcceptedSettlementCompleted [F-PAYMENT-PAYMENT-STATUS]. It is stored in the database [DATA-PAYMENT STORED_IN SYS-DB].

**IdempotencyRegistry** [DATA-IDEMP] holds a key hash, third party, request hash, resource id and expiry, which supports the requirement against second debits [R-05]. It is stored in the database [DATA-IDEMP STORED_IN SYS-DB].

**SecurityEventLog** [DATA-AUDIT] holds event id, actor reference, action, correlation id and recording time, and is flagged as holding personal information; actor_ref is marked personal and confidential [F-AUDIT-ACTOR-REF]. It is stored in Audit and metrics [DATA-AUDIT STORED_IN SYS-OBS]. It is accessed by API ingress [APP-EDGE access DATA-AUDIT].

The data-at-rest control covers all three of ConsentLedger, PaymentLedger and the event log [SEC-SC28], and key management covers the first two [SEC-SC12]. The access classification of ConsentLedger and SecurityEventLog is not known (section 10).

```desnre ax-data
```

```desnre table data
```

### 9.5 Application architecture

Eight application components work together; all are planned. **API ingress** [APP-EDGE] terminates the provider API channel and produces correlated security events. It owns the Payment Initiation API v2.3.3 [IFC-PAYMENT-INITIATION] and passes traffic to the Payments hub [APP-EDGE flow APP-PAYHUB] and to Consent processing [APP-EDGE flow APP-CONSENT]. **Identity** [APP-IDENT] handles customer authentication and passes the outcome to Consent processing [APP-IDENT flow APP-CONSENT]. **Consent processing** [APP-CONSENT] controls the consent lifecycle and its persistence [APP-CONSENT access DATA-CONSENT].

The **Payments hub** [APP-PAYHUB] validates and orchestrates initiation, idempotency, risk, status and retries. It reads and writes consent, payment and idempotency data [APP-PAYHUB access DATA-PAYMENT], calls the Fraud service [APP-PAYHUB flow APP-RISK], the Account ledger [APP-PAYHUB flow APP-LEDGER], the Outbound connector [APP-PAYHUB flow APP-OUTBOUND] and the Notification service [APP-PAYHUB flow APP-NOTIFY], and triggers the Durable handoff event emitted when a payment is recorded as accepted for execution [APP-PAYHUB triggering EVT-HANDOFF]. The **Fraud service** [APP-RISK] returns a risk decision. The **Account ledger** [APP-LEDGER] owns account eligibility and posting and rejects repeated posting ids. The **Outbound connector** [APP-OUTBOUND] performs the accepted-instruction hand-off. The **Notification service** [APP-NOTIFY] is described as a non-critical downstream component.

The API is secured by oauth2 over https and is internet facing [IFC-PAYMENT-INITIATION]. It offers five operations: Create domestic payment consent [API-CONSENT-CREATE], Read domestic payment consent [API-CONSENT-READ], Create domestic payment [API-PAYMENT-CREATE], Read domestic payment [API-PAYMENT-READ] and Read payment debtor account [API-DEBTOR-READ]. The last has method GET but no path or payload fields yet, and is returned only where DebtorAccountRelease is true [R-24].

```desnre ax-application
```

```desnre table apps
```

```desnre table api
```

### 9.6 Technology architecture

Everything runs in one environment, Production [ENV-PROD], at the NZ production location [LOC-NZ], described as fictional. Five nodes sit in five network zones: Redundant API ingress [NODE-EDGE] in the Edge zone, a DMZ [ZONE-EDGE]; Three-node application compute [NODE-APP] in the Application zone [ZONE-APP]; Database nodes [NODE-DATA] in the private Data zone [ZONE-DATA]; Identity and secrets [NODE-SEC] in the private Security zone [ZONE-SEC]; and Ledger and execution integration [NODE-INT] in the Integration zone [ZONE-INTEG].

API ingress is deployed on the ingress node [DEP-EDGE]; Consent processing, the Payments hub, the Fraud service and the Notification service share the application compute [DEP-CONSENT] [DEP-PAYHUB] [DEP-RISK] [DEP-NOTIFY]; Identity is on the identity and secrets node [DEP-IDENT]; and the Account ledger and Outbound connector are on the integration node [DEP-LEDGER] [DEP-OUT]. The application compute also hosts Durable events [SYS-MQ]. The identity and secrets node hosts Managed key custody [SYS-KMS] and Audit and metrics [SYS-OBS]. The database node hosts the Managed database [SYS-DB], described as a fictional PostgreSQL-compatible database with a synchronous local standby and a tested recovery procedure. The Payment Initiation API is exposed through the ingress node [IFC-PAYMENT-INITIATION EXPOSED_THROUGH NODE-EDGE].

Four paths connect nodes: the external boundary path uses https and is encrypted [PATH-EDGE]; the payment hand-off path uses tls and is encrypted [PATH-HANDOFF]; the application-to-database path [PATH-DATA] and the secret retrieval path [PATH-KEY] record neither protocol nor encryption yet. Four deployments lack a platform_id [DEP-CONSENT] [DEP-PAYHUB] [DEP-RISK] [DEP-NOTIFY]. The design holds one location only; it does not say how a second site or recovery location would work.

```desnre ax-technology
```

```desnre table paths
```

### 9.7 Security architecture

The security layer holds 15 controls, 9 threats and 1 trust boundary. Every control has implementation status "planned". SDEM's coverage lists 62 records in scope, of which 22 are protected by a control. Controls are named by their NIST SP 800-53 id.

**S1 business.** Separation of duties, AC-5, protects Post one debit and the Bank — account servicing role [SEC-AC5]; the data records no record that enforces it. Customer authentication, IA-2, protects Authenticate and authorise [SEC-IA2] and is enforced by Identity [APP-IDENT]. The three business actors and six other processes have no control [ACTOR-CUSTOMER] [ACTOR-MERCHANT] [ACTOR-TPP] [PROC-CONSENT] [PROC-VALIDATE] [PROC-RISK] [PROC-SUBMIT] [PROC-HANDOFF] [PROC-STATUS].

```desnre sec-S1
```

**S2 service domains.** Payment Order Initiation [SD-PAYMENT-ORDER-INITIATION] has AC-3, enforced by the Payments hub [SEC-POI-AC3], and AU-10, enforced by Audit and metrics [SEC-POI-AU10]; its control record has SI-7 [SEC-POI-SI7]. Party Authentication [SD-PARTY-AUTHENTICATION] has IA-2 [SEC-IA2] and IA-5 [SEC-PA-IA5]. Fraud Evaluation [SD-FRAUD-EVALUATION] has AC-6 [SEC-FE-AC6] and its assessment record has SI-7 [SEC-FE-SI7], both enforced by the Fraud service [APP-RISK].

```desnre sec-S2
```

**S3 data.** SC-28 protects ConsentLedger, PaymentLedger and the SecurityEventLog and is enforced by the Managed database [SEC-SC28] [DATA-CONSENT] [DATA-PAYMENT] [DATA-AUDIT]. SC-12 protects the first two and is enforced by Managed key custody [SEC-SC12] [SYS-KMS]. IdempotencyRegistry has no control [DATA-IDEMP].

```desnre sec-S3
```

**S4 applications.** IA-8 (OAuth2) protects the Payment Initiation API and is enforced by API ingress [SEC-IA8] [IFC-PAYMENT-INITIATION]. SI-10 protects the two create operations and is enforced by the Payments hub and Consent processing [SEC-SI10] [API-CONSENT-CREATE] [API-PAYMENT-CREATE]. AU-12 protects Consent processing and the Payments hub, enforced by API ingress and Audit and metrics [SEC-AU12]. API ingress itself, Identity, the Fraud service, the Account ledger, the Outbound connector and the Notification service have no PROTECTS link from a control.

```desnre sec-S4
```

**S5 technology.** SC-8 protects all four paths and is enforced by the ingress and integration nodes [SEC-SC8] [PATH-EDGE] [PATH-DATA] [PATH-KEY] [PATH-HANDOFF]. SC-7 protects the Edge zone and is enforced by the ingress node [SEC-SC7] [ZONE-EDGE]. The trust boundary Internet edge bounds the Edge zone, with enforcement recorded as "API ingress (redundant) with OAuth2 and TLS" [TB-INTERNET-EDGE]. The Application, Data, Security and Integration zones have no control [ZONE-APP] [ZONE-DATA] [ZONE-SEC] [ZONE-INTEG].

```desnre sec-S5
```

**Threats and mitigation.** Each of the nine threats is mitigated: impersonation of a third party by IA-8 [THR-SPOOF-TPP]; tampering on the hand-off path by SC-8 [THR-TAMPER-HANDOFF]; consent repudiation by AU-12 [THR-REPUDIATE-CONSENT]; disclosure of consent data by SC-28 and SC-12 [THR-DISCLOSE-CONSENT]; edge flooding by SC-7 [THR-FLOOD-EDGE]; unauthorised payment orders by AC-3 and AU-10 [THR-POI-UNAUTH]; order tampering by SI-7 [THR-POI-TAMPER]; credential compromise by IA-5 [THR-PA-CREDS]; and fraud bypass by SI-7 and AC-6 [THR-FE-BYPASS].

```desnre table security
```

## 10. Gap analysis

**Unconfirmed and unknown.** The completeness standard reports no gaps and no unconfirmed records. SDEM lists six unresolved items and 15 warnings. The unresolved items are all security: access_classification is not known for SecurityEventLog and ConsentLedger [DATA-AUDIT] [DATA-CONSENT], and encryption and protocol are not known for the application-to-database and secret retrieval paths [PATH-DATA] [PATH-KEY]. The warnings include missing path and payload fields on the debtor-account read [API-DEBTOR-READ], missing platform ids on four deployments [DEP-CONSENT] [DEP-PAYHUB] [DEP-RISK] [DEP-NOTIFY], and advice that none of the three service domains is composed into a business domain.

**Unconnected.** Four processes have no service domain or application behind them [PROC-CONSENT] [PROC-VALIDATE] [PROC-DEBIT] [PROC-HANDOFF]. 40 business records, including all requirements, actors and channels, have no connection to another layer; requirements often belong in one layer, so this is not by itself a defect. Two proposed connections were rejected: API ingress realising Payment Order Initiation, and Fraud Evaluation supporting Payment risk control [CAP-RISK]. The Durable events software and the Durable handoff event have no cross-layer link between them [SYS-MQ] [EVT-HANDOFF].

**Not in the data.** The design records the reasons for no decision, no baseline, no business-case figures, and no unhappy paths (fraud rejection, insufficient funds, a failed posting, a duplicate request). No second location or recovery site is recorded [LOC-NZ], although recovery targets are set [R-15]. CIBA authorisation is required but not designed [R-21].

**Security findings from SDEM.** `SEC-S08` is non-compliant on API ingress [APP-EDGE]: a component that accesses personal data has no audit control (AU-2 or AU-12) protecting it. `SEC-S01a` is unresolved on SecurityEventLog and ConsentLedger [DATA-AUDIT] [DATA-CONSENT]. `SEC-S03a` (encryption not known) and `SEC-S03b` (missing protocol) are unresolved on the two paths [PATH-DATA] [PATH-KEY]. No control protects the Application, Data, Security and Integration zones [ZONE-APP] [ZONE-DATA] [ZONE-SEC] [ZONE-INTEG]. No S-layer is empty.

```desnre table security-findings
```

```desnre table traceability
```

```desnre table open
```

## 11. Impact assessment

What relies on each application, as the design's links show: API ingress [APP-EDGE] is the entry point and nothing in the design flows into it. The Payments hub [APP-PAYHUB] is relied on by API ingress [APP-EDGE flow APP-PAYHUB] and realises Payment Order Initiation [MAP-005]. Consent processing [APP-CONSENT] is relied on by API ingress and Identity [APP-EDGE flow APP-CONSENT] [APP-IDENT flow APP-CONSENT]. Identity [APP-IDENT] realises Party Authentication [MAP-006], used by Authenticate and authorise [MAP-003]. The Fraud service [APP-RISK], Account ledger [APP-LEDGER], Outbound connector [APP-OUTBOUND] and Notification service [APP-NOTIFY] are each called only by the Payments hub [APP-PAYHUB flow APP-RISK] [APP-PAYHUB flow APP-LEDGER] [APP-PAYHUB flow APP-OUTBOUND] [APP-PAYHUB flow APP-NOTIFY]. A change to the Payments hub therefore reaches four downstream components, and four applications share one compute node [NODE-APP].

```desnre table impact
```

## Suggestions (not from the design)

These are inferences from reading the design, not facts it records. Each would need confirming and adding to the data.

- **Give the four unowned steps a home.** Capturing consent, validating, debiting and handing off have no service domain connection. The owner could decide which domain or application each belongs to.
- **Design the unhappy paths.** Fraud rejection, insufficient funds, a failed posting and a duplicate request each need a defined outcome and a status the provider can see.
- **Audit the API ingress.** The security finding on API ingress suggests recording an audit control that protects it directly.
- **Complete the path and classification fields.** Record protocol and encryption for the two unresolved paths, and access classification for the consent and event data.
- **Decide on recovery.** The recovery targets may imply a second location; the answer would change the technology architecture.
- **Record the decisions.** The shared compute, event-based hand-off and one-application-per-domain choices should each become a decision with its reason.
- **Add a baseline** if any part replaces an existing service.
